title: Well and Harvest
premise: Freya Amberdale, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards and writes it all down, moves to the village of Hollowmere for a quiet placement at Amberdale House — the estate his estranged family left him. There the melted bell of 1911 rings each dusk, and the dying count toward a date, not a death: the day the last resident signs the inheritance papers. Freya learns his ancestors bought the village's survival with a covenant of names, and that the bell collects what the ledger owes. To save his daughter and the last resident, old Mrs. Ellery-Vane, he must break the covenant — signing the papers himself, taking the debt into his own body — and in the final chapter the bell rings once, for him, while the family escapes ahead of the count.
about_author: Dominic Villalobos is a former parish records clerk from the Pacific Northwest who spent a decade transcribing death registers in rural counties. His fiction blends bureaucratic dread with folk horror, and 'Well and Harvest' is his second novel.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In his final week at the city hospice, Freya documents a dying man counting backwards from 214, and notices the number matches days to a date he doesn't yet understand. He accepts a placement in Hollowmere, his family's ancestral village. Emotional beat: weary professional detachment beginning to crack with dread.

chapters.title: Amberdale House
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. He arrives with his daughter Wren at the decaying estate he inherited, finding a locked well, a ledger of names in the study, and neighbors who won't say his surname aloud. Emotional beat: uneasy wonder curdling into the sense of being expected.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At dusk the church bell rings, though the vicar shows him the 1911 receipt proving it was melted for the war effort. Only Freya and Wren seem to hear it. Emotional beat: gaslit isolation; the first proof he cannot stay invisible.

chapters.title: Mrs. Ellery-Vane's Papers
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. His sole hospice patient, the ancient last resident of Hollowmere, asks him to witness a document — the covenant papers — then refuses to sign. That night the bell rings twice. Emotional beat: the dawning weight of a duty disguised as a favor.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Owed
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, interleaved with ledger entries. He deciphers the family ledger: every generation, an Amberdale signed away a name, and the village harvested a good year. The counting dying were counting to signing day. Emotional beat: horror of inheritance as arithmetic.

chapters.title: What the Well Keeps
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, exploring against orders, drops a stone down the sealed well and hears it never land — only counting. She begins hearing her own name in the water. Emotional beat: childlike curiosity turning to quiet terror she hides from her father.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Confession
chapters.summary: Vicar Halloway's POV. The vicar admits the parish has falsified the bell's destruction for a century; the bell was never melted, only buried beneath the church. He begs Freya to let the covenant run its course. Emotional beat: complicity and cowardice dressed as piety.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Every dying resident of Hollowmere now counts in unison, and the number is small: eleven. Mrs. Ellery-Vane's mind clears long enough to tell him the bell rings for whoever is owed. Emotional beat: urgency compressing; the horror becomes a deadline.

chapters.title: The Harvest Record
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, with archival documents. In the county archive Freya finds the 1911 harvest record: the year the bell 'died,' the village's crops failed and eleven people starved — the price of a broken covenant. Emotional beat: the past proving the stakes are literal.

chapters.title: Neighbors at the Gate
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Villagers gather at Amberdale House, polite and terrible, asking Freya to sign the papers 'for everyone's sake.' He refuses; that night every clock in the house runs backwards. Emotional beat: the community revealed as a congregation of the debt.

chapters.title: Wren's Name in the Water
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The well calls Wren by name; she writes it in her school notebook and the ink runs upward like something climbing. Freya realizes the covenant will take a name from his line regardless. Emotional beat: a parent's terror sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Buried Bell
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya and the vicar dig beneath the church floor and find the bell, un-melted, its surface engraved with thousands of names — the newest still wet. Touching it, Freya hears his own name added. Emotional beat: awe and violation; the artifact is alive with the owed.

chapters.title: Mrs. Ellery-Vane Signs
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Broken by fear, Mrs. Ellery-Vane signs the papers at last — but the bell does not stop, because her signature only names the next Amberdale: Freya. Emotional beat: betrayal of hope; the trap's true mechanism revealed.

chapters.title: The Count Reaches One
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The dying count reaches one. The village goes silent at dusk — no bell, no birds, no wind — a held breath. Wren packs her father's documentation, refusing to leave without him. Emotional beat: stillness before catastrophe; love as defiance.

chapters.title: Reading the Covenant
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya reads the covenant's full terms: a signed name feeds the bell for a generation, but a name given freely, with the debt accepted in full, ends it — at the cost of the signer. Emotional beat: the terrible arithmetic of a way out.

chapters.title: What Documentation Is For
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya writes his final entry — everything he knows, for Wren — understanding that documentation was never prayer but a will: a way to survive as testimony. Emotional beat: transfiguration of his compulsion into purpose and farewell.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Mrs. Ellery-Vane's POV. The old woman, dying, tells Freya she was the one who let the covenant lapse in 1911's shadow out of spite, and asks his forgiveness — the bell rings for her first. Emotional beat: guilt, apology, and the dignity of a small, late honesty.

chapters.title: Getting Them Out
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya puts Wren on the morning bus with the ledger and his notebooks, lying that he'll follow, as the villagers watch with something like pity. Emotional beat: heartbreak disguised as logistics; the price of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At dusk Freya signs the covenant in his own name, accepting the debt entire. The bell rings once, sweet and enormous, and the well exhales a century of counting. Emotional beat: sacrificial calm; the climax's terrible relief.

chapters.title: Hollow Bells
chapters.summary: Vicar Halloway's POV. The village wakes to ordinary silence. The bell is found cracked and finally mute; the ledger's pages are blank. Halloway buries it properly and lies in his register one last time — that there was never a bell. Emotional beat: exhausted grace; the machinery of denial resuming.

chapters.title: What Wren Counts
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Weeks later, in a city hospice where she volunteers, Wren hears a dying woman counting — forwards. She reads her father's notebooks aloud to the dying, and they stop counting and listen. Emotional beat: grief metabolized into inheritance of a better kind.

chapters.title: The Final Entry
chapters.summary: Freya's voice, posthumous, as the notebook's last pages. A final entry written in a hand that trails off mid-sentence, describing dusk, the bell's single note, and the feeling of being counted at last — and found sufficient. Emotional beat: haunting peace; the horror and the mercy are the same thing.
